candidates.context: Previous Exploration The Yangibana ironstones were first pegged by a prospecting syndicate in 1972, as base metal-bearing banded ironstone targets. Recorded uranium exploration commenced in 1973 when Noranda Australia Limited (Noranda) investigated an ironstone outcrop with an elevated total count radiometric response (the Yangibana or Noranda Gossan) identified through ground scintillometer traversing and surface geochemical sampling. Maximum uranium values of 53ppm U for an ironstone and 71ppm U for feldspathic wallrock were recorded.

2. Introduction


 During 2018 a total of 372 drillholes were completed on the Yangibana Project, for a total of 20,126.05m, including 2969.05m of diamond
 drilling.  Drilling at Bald Hill and Fraser’s was predominantly designed to provide sample for a pilot plant programme, with drilling at Auer
 and Auer North completed for resource definition and expansion.
 Geotechnical drilling (DD) was carried out in Yangibana, Auer and Auer North. 19 geotechnical holes were drilled for a total of 1887.4m
 which is included in the total metres quoted above. This drilling was completed for ongoing mining studies to allow conversion of resources
 to reserves.
 Following completion of drilling the Mineral Resource Estimate for the project was updated, and now stands at 21.67 Mt @ 1.17% TREO
 including 0.40% Nd2O3 Pr6O11.
 Further geophysical modelling and processing was completed utilising the airborne magnetic data acquired during 2016. This work focused
 on extensions to Auer and Auer North, and surrounding areas. Inversion modelling of the southern extension to Auer led to successful drill
 testing.
 The geophysical modelling also identified a large, deep target in the southeast of the project area. This target, currently termed T1, is
 scheduled for drill testing in 2019.
 Metallurgical work continued throughout the year on various samples.
An Exploration Index Plan is provided as Figure 1.

3. Location and Access Details


 The Yangibana Project is located approximately 270 kilometres east northeast of Carnarvon, within the Upper Gascoyne Shire of Western
 Australia (Figure 2). The project is predominantly located within the Edmund 1:250,000 map sheet, with the southern portion of the project
 area located upon the Mt Phillips 1:250,000 map sheet.
 Access is by sealed road from Carnarvon to Gascoyne Junction, and then by gravel road from Gascoyne Junction to Gifford Creek
 Homestead. Numerous station tracks provide access within the project area.

5. Geology

5.1 Regional Geology


 The Yangibana Project covers a majority of the Gifford Creek Ferrocarbonatite Suite (GCFS; Johnson, 2013). The GCFS is located within the
 Gascoyne Province of the Capricorn Orogen, between the Archaean Yilgarn Craton to the south, and the Archaean Pilbara Craton to the
 north. The Gascoyne Province, which consists of a suite of Archaean to Proterozoic gneisses, granitic and metasedimentary rocks (Johnson
 et al, 2011), is overlain by the Paleoproterozoic Ashburton Formation to the north, the Mesoproterozoic Edmund and Collier Basins to the
 east, and the Phanerozoic Carnarvon Basin to the west.

5.2 Local Geology


 Locally the tenement area consists of granitic rocks of the 1680-1620 Ma Durlacher Supersuite, specifically the Pimbyana and Yangibana
 Granites, which contain abundant rafts of sedimentary rocks including arenites, calc-silicates, and quartzites of the 1760-1680 Ma Pooranoo
 Metamorphics. These rocks are intruded by sills, dykes, and veins of ferrocarbonatite and ironstone, and associated fenitic alteration, which
 comprise the 1,300-1,280 Ma GCFS (Figure 3; Johnson, 2013).
 The area has been subject to several distinct tectonothermal cycles of which the Mangaroon Orogeny (1680-1620Ma), the Mutherbukin
 Tectonic Event (1385-1200Ma) and the Edmundian Orogen (1030-955Ma) are the most significant. During the Mangaroon Orogeny, intense
 deformation and metamorphism were coincident with the intrusion of the Durlacher Supersuite (Wallace and Mortimer, 2016; Slezak, 2017).
 The ferrocarbonatites that occur within the project area have been dated at 1262-986Ma, which are coincident with both the Mutherbukin
 Tectonic Event and the Edmundian Orogeny. The Lyons River Fault, which is a deep crustal lineament that has been traced to the
 Mohorovicic discontinuity, may have acted as a fluid conduit during these events, resulting in the emplacement of the ferrocarbonatites and
 associated hydrothermal alteration over a period of several hundred million years (Slezak, 2017).
 The GCFS is dominated by two major southeast trending shear zones, which are cross-cut by multiple north-south to north-east trending
 faults. The Northern Shear Zone, the Bald Hill Lineament, is anastomosing and variable in width, comprising multiple fault splays (Wallace
 and Mortimer, 2016). Geophysical interpretation by Southern Geoscience Consultants during 2016 indicated that the Bald Hill Lineament
 separates an early, highly fractured granite to the north from folded Pooranoo Metamorphics to the south.
 The southern shear zone, the Lyons River Fault, is less complex and narrow, forming the boundary between the Edmund Group, and an
 early granite to the north. A third major shear zone is evident in the geophysical data trending east-west to east-southeast (Wallace and
 Mortimer, 2016).
 The Pooranoo Metamorphics are multiple folded along southeast trending axes. In the northwest these folds are generally wide with granite
 cores. This area of wider folding has also been intruded by a later granite. In general, the metamorphics are more highly deformed toward
 the east (Wallace and Mortimer, 2016).

One of the key features of the GCFS within the project area is the widespread occurrence of ironstone dykes that are spatially associated with
 the ferrocarbonatite intrusions. These are surrounded by relatively narrow haloes of fenitic alteration, and locally associated with quartz
 veining (Johnson, 2013).  Fenitic alteration haloes are characterised by the presence of feldspars and/or Na-amphiboles and magnetite. The
 ironstone dykes, with dominant north, northeast and west-northwest trends, consist predominantly of goethite, hematite, and magnetite, and
 are locally weakly radioactive. The ferrocarbonatites and ironstones of the GCFS occur as sinuous pods and veins generally less than 10m
 wide, that are traceable for up to 25 kilometres. The ironstones of the GCFS have historically been the focus of exploration activity in the
 area, due to their enrichment in Rare Earths Elements (REE).
 The main ore mineral at Yangibana is monazite. The monazite occurs in the ironstone dykes, and are considered to be the weathered
 remnants of the ferrocarbonatite intrusions and related rock types. Two distinct types of carbonatite have been identified within the project
 area as described by Slezak, 2017:

   1. Fine grained dolomitic carbonatites predominantly in the south of the project area near the Lyons River Fault
   2. Macro-crystalline ferrocarbonatites found at depth proximal to ironstones that occur sub-parallel to the Lyons River Fault

 The fine grained dolomitic carbonatites are composed predominantly of dolomite, aegirine, riebeckite, magnetite, and apatite with lesser
 barite and monazite. The macro-crystalline ferrocarbonatites are associated with the ore bearing ironstones. They are composed of coarse
 ankerite and subordinate calcite, with inclusions and veins of biotite, magnetite, monazite, apatite, and minor potassium feldspar. Phoscorite
 has also been identified associated with the ore-bearing ironstones, composed of biotite, magnetite, apatite, and monazite (Slezak, 2017).
 The potential for the presence of carbonatite and associated intrusions to be present at depth is supported by petrological analysis of samples
 from both outcrop and drilling which has identified both phoscorite and carbonatite as hosts to mineralisation. This work has indicated that
 the outcropping ironstones throughout the Yangibana project area may in fact be the weathered and leached remnants of phoscorite
 intrusions associated with the GCFS. Mineralisation hosted by ferroan dolomite or ankeritic carbonate as identified in drilling, may have
 exsolved from the phoscoritic parent magma (Crawford, 2016).  Identification of these lithologies suggests that there is good potential for
 further primary mineralisation to be identified at depth below the current level of drilling associated with the phoscorite and/or carbonatite
 units.
 REE mineralisation at Yangibana is predominantly hosted by monazite, a phosphate mineral.  Initial petrological assessment of samples of
 mineralised carbonatite from Yangibana North, identified the monazite as being the Ce rich endmember monazite-(Ce). With the acquisition
 of further data from other areas within the project area, significant variations in the Nd content from prospect to prospect were identified.
 Prospects in the Eastern Belt of mineralisation (Bald Hill, Fraser’s, Auer, and Auer North) were identified as having significantly higher Nd
 content than prospects within the Western Belt of mineralisation (Yangibana to Kane’s Gossan) suggesting that monazite may vary
 throughout the project area from the monazite-(Ce) variant, toward more Nd rich variants (monazite-(Nd)).

6. Previous Exploration





 The Yangibana ironstones were first pegged by a prospecting syndicate in 1972, as base metal-bearing banded ironstone targets.
 Recorded uranium exploration commenced in 1973 when Noranda Australia Limited (Noranda) investigated an ironstone outcrop with an
 elevated total count radiometric response (the Yangibana or Noranda Gossan) identified through ground scintillometer traversing and surface
 geochemical sampling. Maximum uranium values of 53ppm U for an ironstone and 71ppm U for feldspathic wallrock were recorded. As
 Noranda decided that the radiometric anomalism was largely due to thorium they undertook no further exploration.
 From 1974 to 1975 Newmont Pty Ltd (Newmont) explored the area for base metals and focused on five prospects within their tenements and
 the surrounding area. Work consisted of rock chip sampling and diamond drilling. Results from rock chip sampling identified lead-zinc rich
 gossans of up to 3% Pb and 1% Zn, with uranium levels of up to 58ppm U at Yangibana East (Noranda Gossan), South Yangibana
 (Yangibana South), and East Fraser’s Well (Fraser’s) prospects. Diamond drilling at the South Yangibana and East Fraser’s Well prospects
 intersected base metal mineralisation of up to 0.65% Zn, 0.55% Pb, and 5g/t Ag hosted by a carbonate-rich magnetite-muscovite schist.
 Analyses for the diamond drilling programme did not include uranium.
 In 1981 Cliffs International Incorporated first examined the area for manganese before subsequent photogeological studies identified
 additional targets for base metals and uranium. One report indicates that 63 rock chip samples were collected and resulting assays recorded
 anomalous lead, zinc and REE. No records of this sampling have been identified.
 Between 1985 and 1991 Challenger Mining Corporation NL and Hurlston Pty Ltd (Challenger; Hurlston) carried out rock chip sampling,
 mapping, petrology, ground radiometrics and reverse circulation (RC) drilling. In the 1987 Annual Report for E09/95, Challenger reported
 secondary uranium mineralisation associated with ironstone veins. Surface samples from five main prospects returned up to 1.41% U within
 ironstone, and up to 0.16% U in granitic wall rocks. REE values were considered to be highly anomalous with up to 1.68% Ce, 0.77% La,
 and 0.16% Nd reported.  Details of analytical methods or laboratories, and exact sample locations have not been identified.
 In 1988 Challenger drilled a total of 80 RC drillholes across ten REE prospects along a total strike length of seven kilometres. Challenger
 calculated average grade and bulk mineralisation tonnage for each prospect which was then totalled into an ‘indicated shallow resource
 potential’ of over 3.5 million tonnes at 1.7% rare earth oxide (pre-JORC estimate).  It was acknowledged that further drilling was required,
 however this was never undertaken.
Newmont (later Newcrest Mining NL) resumed exploration of the area in 1989, in a joint venture with Western Rare Earths NL. Although no
 further prospects were identified, Newcrest recognised the potential of the Gifford Creek Alkaline Complex and initiated a joint research
 programme with the Key Centre for Strategic Mineral Deposits, University of WA, which culminated in a PhD thesis published in 1996
 (Pearson, 1996).
 In 2007, Vistarise Limited reviewed the available geophysical data and historic exploration, and concluded that the area warranted modern
 multi-commodity exploration.
 During 2008, GTI Resources Ltd (GTI) completed an open file data compilation and a 56-sample rock chip sampling program over selected
 sites.  Multi-client airborne magnetic and radiometric survey data was also reprocessed and reinterpreted. The overall arithmetic average of
 the 56 samples collected by GTI was 2.84% TREO. Results from this rock chip sampling programme confirmed REE mineralisation at
 selected locations. Elevated uranium content previously reported to be associated with ironstones and granitic wall rock by previous explorers
 was not confirmed.
 In 2010, Artemis Resources Ltd (Artemis) undertook a rock and soil sampling program targeting the known east-west striking ironstone
 lenses. The soil samples were collected from below the last indication of plant matter, generally at approximately 20-40cm depth, with the
 rock samples taken at the same location. The programme consisted of a series of north trending transects, each 50 metres in length, with a
 sample collected every 5 metres along each transect. 41 samples of rock and 72 samples of soil were collected. Transects were located at
 the beginning, end, and middle of each targeted zone. A total of 10 transects were completed across four prospects comprising Yangibana
 North, Lion’s Ear, Hook, and immediately to the west of Hook.
 During April of 2010 REE specialist Dr Tony Mariano accompanied Artemis personnel on a site visit. Dr Mariano acquired rock samples for
 scientific studies and completed a report on the economic potential of the Yangibana Project. In July 2010 Artemis completed an auger
 drilling programme comprising the collection of 382 samples. The sampling program incorporated both rock and soil at Yangibana. The
 best results reported were 1.32% Ce, 0.58% La, 0.39% Nd, 0.12% Pr, 649 ppm Sm, and 759ppm Th.




 During September 2011 Hastings Rare Metals Limited undertook an introductory site visit to the Yangibana Project. The trip successfully
 accessed the western portion of the known ironstone outcrop between Yangibana North in the west and Lion’s Ear in the east, and also
 included the southern prospects comprising Tongue, Yangibana and Yangibana South. Thirty-eight grab samples were collected during the
 visit and were analysed by Genalysis Perth, with assays being in line with expectations based on previous exploration. The most consistently
 high results were returned from Lion’s Ear where four of the five samples collected returned TREO grades exceeding 1%, up to a maximum
 of 12.8% TREO, by far the highest assay returned from the programme.

 These results identified a distinct variation between the Western Belt that was sampled between Yangibana North and Lion’s Ear, and the
 southern prospects between Tongue, Yangibana, and Yangibana South. The higher TREO grades appear to occur in the north, but the
 higher (Nd2O3 Pr6O11):TREO ratios were found to occur in the southern prospects.

A second site visit was carried out by Hastings in April 2012 to locate and sample the remaining ironstone outcrops that had not been
 accessed during the site visit in September 2011. Prospects visited during this visit were Hook and Kane’s Gossan. Hook South was not
 reached during the visit. As with the previous visit, a scintillometer was used to identify areas with the highest radiation values on the
 assumption that high radioactive content (Th-U) correlates with high REE content. Grab samples were collected during the visit and analysed
 by Genalysis Perth. The best results returned were 3.58% TREO including 0.85% Nd2O3 Pr6O11 at Hook, and 1.96% TREO including
0.50% Nd2O3 Pr6O11 at Kane’s Gossan.

 During 2014 Hastings completed two drilling programs. The first of these programmes was completed during May 2014, and consisted of
 1,836m of RC drilling across 44 drillholes.  All drillholes completed during this programme were located at the Yangibana North prospect.
 These drillholes were completed across 9 lines in a northeasterly orientation, with drillholes completed at a nominal 50 metre spacing.
 Drillholes ranged in depth from 12 metres to 90 metres.

All holes completed during this programme intersected the target ironstone/quartz unit, surrounded by an alteration halo of fenitised granite
 of variable thickness. The ironstone unit was found to be flat-dipping toward the south and remained open both along strike and at depth.

 Following the success of the RC drilling completed during May 2014, a second drilling programme was completed between August and
 October 2014. This drilling was completed across 8 distinct prospects within the Yangibana Project, comprising Yangibana North, Gossan,
 Lion’s Ear, Hook, Kane’s Gossan, Bald Hill North, Bald Hill South, and Fraser’s.  Drilling had been planned for Yangibana South but was not
 completed. This drilling programme consisted of 6,582 metres of RC drilling, and 171.45 metres of diamond drilling. A total of 116
 drillholes were completed comprising 107 RC drillholes, 6 RC pre-collars with diamond tails, and 3 diamond drillholes from surface.

A total of 70 rock chip samples were collected from regional targets during May 2014. Of these 70 samples, 36 were collected from
 carbonatite sills, ironstone units, and fenitic alteration zones in the southwest of the project area, where only limited work has previously
 been completed. The aim of this sampling was to confirm that the carbonatite sills and fenitic alteration zones carried anomalous REE
 mineralisation, and whether the ironstone outcrops in the area warranted further investigation. Results from these samples indicated that the
 carbonatite sills were anomalous in REE, however due to the generally narrow widths, and low grade, are not currently considered priority
 targets for further exploration in the short term.

 32 samples were collected in the Bald Hill area, 28 of which were collected from the main Bald Hill ironstone outcrop. Of this 28 samples, 19
 returned assays of above 0.5% TREO, with a maximum of 6.06% TREO including 2.71% Nd2O3. Six of these samples also returned greater
 than 5,000 ppm Nb, with a maximum of 66,010 ppm Nb2O5.

 Digital aerial photography and DTM surveying was completed in during late 2014. This resulted in high resolution aerial photography across
 the target prospects within the Yangibana Project, the generation of a detailed DTM to be utilised in resource estimation.

 Phase 3 Drilling was completed between May-August 2015 and consisted of 268 drillholes. This comprised 248 RC drillholes, and 20
 diamond drillholes.  Drilling focused on Bald Hill South, Fraser’s, and Yangibana West. Drilling at Fraser’s and Bald Hill South was focused on
 extending mineralisation identified during Phase 2 drilling along strike, and at depth.  Drilling at Yangibana West focused on testing
 mineralisation directly along strike to the northwest of Yangibana North.

 Additional work completed during 2015 included updated resource estimation, the collection of 22 rock chip samples, geological mapping at
 Bald Hill and Fraser’s, petrographic analysis of six diamond core samples, ongoing metallurgical testwork, and various geotechnical,
 hydrogeological, environmental, and financial studies forming part of a Pre-Feasibility Study for the Yangibana Project.

Two field visits were completed in December 2015 and January 2016, with the aim of sampling a number of new target areas. These field
 visits focused on and area to the southwest of Fraser’s where GSWA mapping indicated a number of ironstone veins. Rock chip sampling in
 this area retuned up to 1.90% (Nd2O3 Pr6O11) and 3.67% TREO. Importantly, the rock chip samples in this area indicated that the
 ironstone units have a high (Nd2O3 Pr6O11)/TREO ratio, similar to the higher value deposits at Bald Hill and Fraser’s. The most promising
 ironstone units identified from this sampling were named Auer, Mosander, Demarcay, Leceq, and Hisinger and prioritised for drill testing.

 During 2016, 305 drillholes were completed for a total of 15,090.29m.  Drilling was focused on Bald Hill and Fraser’s and was designed as
 infill drilling with the aim of upgrading the previous Indicated resource areas to Measured category. A number of new targets were also drill
 tested, which had been identified through the earlier geochemical sampling, and available geophysics. These new targets comprised Auer,
 Auer North, Mosander, Demarcay, and Hatchett. Updated resource estimation was subsequently completed following the 2016 drilling
 programme.

 Minor diamond drilling for geotechnical purposes was also completed over areas proposed for tailings storage facilities, and the processing
 plant within E09/2007 and E09/2018 respectively, as part of the ongoing Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS).

 During June and July of 2016, high resolution airborne magnetic and radiometric data was acquired over the Yangibana Project (Registration
 ID R71264). Acquisition was completed by Thomson Aviation, with 17,908 line kilometres of data acquired at a line spacing of 25m.
 Processing and interpretation was completed by Southern Geoscience Consultants (SGC). SGC identified 108 thorium anomalies within the
 radiometric dataset, with 22 areas identified as priorities for further exploration.

 Digital aerial photography and DTM surveying was also completed during 2016 by HyVista Corporation, to extend the existing survey area as
 completed in 2014 (Registration ID R71266). The data acquired in 2016 was merged with the 2014 survey, to provide DTM and airphoto
 coverage over new target areas, and areas of proposed mining infrastructure.

 During 2017 a total of 451 drillholes were completed on the Yangibana Project, for a total of 30,025.94m, including 3105.94m of diamond
 drilling (Figure 5).  Drilling included resource definition and extension drilling at Bald Hill, Fraser’s Yangibana North, Yangibana West, Auer,
 and Auer North, exploration drilling at Terry’s Find, Yangibana, and Simon’s Find, and a programme of water exploration drilling. This
 drilling resulted in updates to Resource estimations for areas with existing Resources, and initial resource estimation for Yangibana and
 Simon’s Find.

 Further rock chip sampling, XRD mineralogical analysis, and petrological analysis were also completed during 2017.

8.6 Petrology


 In the first petrographic report 24 rocks from two prospects, Spider Hill (7 samples) and Simon’s Find (17 samples), were examined. A
 1.25hr microprobe session at UTAS Central Science Laboratory was carried to confirm the composition of the extremely fine-grained phases
 in a number of ironstone samples which could not be confidently identified petrographically.
 The samples from Spider Hill included 3 veined, medium-grained monzonites with well developed ‘ironstone’ veining, a foliated syenite to
 microsyenite, a contact between a micromonzonite and an aplite, two entirely metasomatic rocks and a banded fault zone rock composed
 almost entirely of smashed vein quartz and Fe oxy-hydroxides. The monzonites have K-spar megacrysts or coarse phenocrysts up to 1cm
 long, and all three monzonites show a heavily fractured fabric, with seams and veinlets of pale brown phlogopite and scattered magnetite
 euhedra apparently invading along fractures and grains boundaries.
 Samples from Simon’s find ranged from heavily fractured quartz veins with either colourless clays or red Fe oxy-hydroxides filling voids and
 openings along fractures to very even-textured, strongly weathered and altered ironstone composed almost entirely of fine-grained quartz
 and magnetite that is now almost entirely replaced by hematite and Fe oxy-hydroxides.
 A total of 14 samples from drillholes at Auer were submitted to A & A Crawford Geological Research Consultants for petrographical
 analysis. The samples examined were obtained from holes AUDD178, AUDD182 and AURC198. The rocks from AUDD178 and AUDD182
 are all phoscorite-syenite association rocks. The RC chips in 5 slides prepared from the three 1m intervals between 49m and 52 m in hole
 AURC198 were found to contain only regolithic Fe oxy-hydroxide material, vein quartz and weathered siliceous banded Fe formation
 metasediments, with no chips from phoscorite-syenite association rocks; these were of no further interest.
 The reports provided by A & A Crawford Geological Research Consultants are provided as appendices.

8.7 XRD Analysis


 Utilisation of the Company’s pXRD equipment has continued to prove invaluable in determining relationships between minerals associated
 with the ore body. Adding to its value in distinguishing between the ironstone hosted mineralisation and the siderite hosted mineralisation,
 a new theory has formed regarding the relationship between the monazite and the presence of Al-phosphates.  It is now believed some of
 the Al-phosphates are present as a result of alteration and hydration of the monazite in some clay rich samples.
 The primary focus this year was on samples from Auer and Auer North with slightly more emphasis being put on the halo of the
 mineralisation.
 Use of the pXRD will continue in 2019 with hopes of gathering more evidence regarding the pre-mentioned theory and discovering new
 mineral relationships involved with the ore body.

8.8 Metallurgy


 Metallurgy was one of the primary reasons for the bulk of the drilling completed in Bald Hill and Fraser’s with the samples collected from the
 RC drilling being used to test how the processing plant will cope with the complexity of the ore body. The beneficiation process was carried
 out at ALS metallurgy’s commercial lab in Balcatta where 19 tonnes of ore collected from this drilling programme was processed. The plant
 was operating for 24 hours a day for 8 days to process the ore.
 Comminution samples were also taken from all diamond holes completed in Bald Hill and Fraser’s, as well as from all non-geotechnical
 diamond holes in Yangibana, Auer and Auer North.
 Further metallurgical tests will have to be carried out on samples from Auer and Auer North to determine variability.

8.9 Geophysical Processing


 During 2018 Southern Geoscience Consultants was engaged to perform further processing of airborne magnetic data acquired during 2016.


8. Current Exploration Summary                    Page 17 of 21                                          Printed: 6/2/2019

This processing was focused on six target areas proximal to the Auer and Auer North deposits. This processing utilised a combination of
 inversion modelling, forward modelling, and depth filtering to better define magnetic targets.
 The inversion modelling was successful in modelling a feature with a strong magnetic susceptibility over a strike length of approximately 1
 kilometre, with a depth extent of 800m (Figure 12; Figure 13). An application for co-funding through the Exploration Incentive Scheme
 was made for drill testing of this target (T1) and subsequently granted, with drilling planned for 2019.
 Forward modelling was used to provide modelled conductors for a series of discrete linear magnetic features. The most significant of these
 were the strike extensions to Auer to the south, and Auer North to the north, where outcrop is lost below cover. Modelling identified
 tabular bodies broadly consistent with the Auer and Auer North orebodies in both directions. Drill testing of the southern strike extension of
 Auer was completed during 2018, successfully intersecting mineralisation (Figure 10).
 Depth filtering was also implemented to enhance a series of magnetic features in the area, with further follow up work required.
 The report provided by Southern Geoscience Consultants is provided as an Appendix.

9. Conclusion and Recommendations


 Infill drilling completed during 2018 was successful in converting resources into reserves in some of the primary prospects, Bald Hill,
 Fraser’s, Auer and Auer North. The drill programme was also successful in generating the amount of metallurgical sample necessary to carry
 out the test with the pilot plant.
A minor increase to resources was achieved due to an extension of the drilling to the south of Auer.
 The geotechnical drilling programme with holes in Auer, Auer North and Yangibana was completed successfully.
 Further drilling is planned for 2019 with the first 2 holes of the programme testing an aeromagnetic target with a strike length of 1km and a
 strong magnetic susceptibility. These holes will far exceed the depth of any previous holes in the area.
